messages.subject: Re: Question about CODEX analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Noemie,

See my replied below. Thanks for your interest in CODEX and hopefully it is of help.

Yuchao

> On Jun 28, 2017, at 8:43 AM, Noemie Leblay <leb...@students.iarc.fr> wrote:
>

> Hi Yuchao,
>
> Hope this email find you well.
>
> Just to remind you, I used CODEX for WES data using case/control analysis.
> I have some questions about the results:
> 1-      Why in you github repository did you removed the pValue?

Those p-values are calculated based on a simple chi-square test and usually the p-values for the CNVs that are called by CODEX reside in the extreme end towards 0. We are not sure if this is a robust statistics and thus remove it.

> 2-      I would like to analyze the CODEX results using GISTIC2.0. For this I used the IGV script that you performed to obtain a GISTIC compatible files. But it seems that when a sample have no CN information, all the region is removing for all the samples. I would like to know how can I obtained all the CN information from CODEX (including netral event). Did you have any idea where we can change the CODEX segmentation code to obtained all CN that covered our bed?

CODEX don’t return copy number calls in the CN-neutral regions.You can however obtain these based on the normalization and segmentation output.

Y_qc is the raw depth after QC.
Yhat[[optK]] is the normalized read depth after QC.
The copy number calls across exons in all samples are stored in the matrix:  2*Y_qc/Yhat[[optK]]
The segmentation results are output in the table which you have.
For a specific sample, you know which regions don’t harbor CNVs. For these regions, you use 2*(sum(Y_qc))/sum(Yhat[[optK]]) to get the copy number call.

An easy shortcut is to set all copy neutral regions to have copy number 2. This way, you can just use the segment output directly to get those regions (with copy number 2).

> 3-      I am also interested to know how you analyze the CODEX results, did you used GISTIC2.0 or another software? All your comments  are welcome to help me in analysis CNV.

Not sure what you meant by analyzing the CODEX results, I only used R for downstream analysis after calling (i.e., finding incidence rates for specific genomic regions) and have not sured GISTIC before.

>
> Best regards
>
> Noémie Leblay

>
>
>

> To: Noemie Leblay
> Cc: Lynnette Fernandez Cuesta; Nicolas Alcala; CODEX: COpy number Detection by EXome sequencing
> Subject: Re: Question about CODEX analysis
>
> Hi Noemie,
>
> Thanks and no problem! We welcome all questions! We use that to cap the copy numbers but if you like you can of course remove that line and source the function after loading CODEX. The reason that we remove that is because sometimes we want to visualize the copy numbers returned by CODEX and very large copy numbers distorts the range of the plot, for example. Also, in cancer genomics, we categorize any copy number alteration event with copy number >=4 as high gain so all the events will be counted as high gain as compared to gain.
>
> Hope that this clarifies!
> Yuchao
>
>

> >
> > Sorry we have another question for you.
> > We checked your script in the segment function and we saw “chat[chat > 5] <- 5” (line 38). Why do you limit the duplication copy number to 5? Do you have a methodologic/ biological reason? (we know that the other CNV analysis methods can give larger copy number estimates).
> >
> > Thank you so much in advance.
> >
> > Best regards
> >
> >
> > Noémie & Nicolas

> > From: Jiang, Yuchao [mailto:yuc...@wharton.upenn.edu]

> > Subject: RE: Question about CODEX analysis
> >
> > Hi Noemie,
> >
> > To determine the number of latent factors is an active research area in statistics and is non-trivial. We included AIC, BIC, and RSS in CODEX to help the users make the optimal choice. However, sometimes as you said, none of these three metrics give an clear solution. From our experiences we also see sometimes they are monotonic and sometimes there is a sudden valley or peak due to the algorithm not converging. You should definitely not choose a optK at values where the algorithm doesn’t converge, for example, K=6 and 7 from chr7. For your dataset, I would probably go with optK=2 and since all chromosomes from the genome/exome are processed in the same batch, ideally this optimal choice should be the same for all chromosomes. We separate the analysis by chromosome to speed up computation, to help the algorithm converge, and to perform segmentation within each chromosome. With this said, we always load our final segmentation results from CODEX to a genome viewer, IGV for example, and look for regions where we know there are germline/somatic CNVs expected. You may want to try different optK values and see if the signals are these places are successfully recovered.
> >
> > Finally, since you have normal tumor samples and you use the normalize2 function with the normal index as an argument, the exon-wise latent factor is essentially only estimated using the normal samples. Therefore, the choice of optK doesn’t have too much effect on the calling of somatic CNV events. This is what we see from our experience too.
> >
> > Hope that this clarifies!
> >
> > Cheers,
> > Yuchao
> >
> >
> >

> >
> > I hope this email find you well.
> > Sorry I have some others questions for you.
> >
> > I (together with my supervisor Lynnette and coworker Nicolas; CC) ran 55 cases-controls (110 samples total) using recommended parameters for qc function, and the normalize2 function with a number of latent Poisson factors between 1 and 10. I obtained some RSS, AIC, and BIC pdf files that are similar to your example (see chr1), that is, a monotonically decreasing RSS as a function of K, a BIC with an elbow where the optimal K is obvious.
> >
> > Nevertheless, I also obtain weird RSS, AIC, and BIC values. I have two types of weird results. First, ones where the AIC and BIC increase monotonically over the specified range of K, or plateau after a threshold value of K (see Chr3). I guess these correspond to cases where the K value maximizing the AIC is >10, but I am not sure if it is a good idea to increase K too much, especially when the slope of the BIC is small. Second, ones where the AIC and BIC present “dips” (see Chr6 and 7). I guess these are cases where the maximum likelihood algorithm did not converge properly for some K values. I tried tuning the threshold values for beta hat and h hat in the normalize2 function to force a better convergence; it did reduce the size of the dips, but they are still there.
> >
> > Did you ever see something of the sort in your previous tests? Do you have recommendations regarding the way to find the optimal K when BIC do not provide a clear answer? How much does the value of K influence the results in such cases and how can we be sure to obtain conservative results?
> >
> > Thank you so much in advance.
> >
> > Best regards
> >
> >

Start_bp end_bp copy_number
1000 2000 3
5000 7000 1
12000 14000 1

The  you know from 2001 to 4999 has copy number 2. From 7001 to 11999 has copy number 2 also, You can get the corresponding raw depths and normalized depths from Y_qc and Yhat[[optK]]. You can also get the z-score from the ratio of the two.
